extracted.intended_audience: Design patent applicants and intellectual property practitioners (US and international) considering or handling Hague Agreement filings
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on filing and prosecuting international design patent applications under the Hague Agreement, with emphasis on US practice and interactions with member jurisdictions. Covers procedural changes, exam practice impacts, and practical recommendations for applicants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single international design application filing
rubrics_metrics.description: A US applicant will be able to file a single international design patent application with the International Bureau and use that application to enter all jurisdictions which participate in the Hague Agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether filing through WIPO or an office of indirect filing such as the USPTO, the applicant files one application and pays fees for each jurisdiction to be entered. In many jurisdictions it may be possible to limit or bypass the use of local counsel, thereby decreasing overall filing costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design patent term change (14 to 15 years)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Hague Agreement increases the term of US Design patents from 14 years to 15 years from the issue date on applications filed on or after May 13, 2015.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This extra year of term applies to all US design patents regardless of whether they are filed through the Hague system or not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility for provisional rights for published international design applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Published WIPO international design patent applications will be eligible for provisional rights in the US, assuming other requirements of 35 U.S.C. § 154(d) are met.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provisional rights require meeting statutory conditions such as providing actual notice of the published patent application to the relevant party. Previously design applications were not eligible because they did not publish until issuance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elimination of petition/fee for color drawings (Rule 1.84(a)(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: Amending Rule 1.84(a)(2) eliminates the petition and fee for color drawings or photographs in design applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although the petition/fee is removed, it is unclear how Examiners will treat applications that do not contain line drawings during examination; applicants should be cautious about relying on color/photographic-only submissions until practice becomes clearer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expedited examination for certain international design applications (Rule 1.155)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule 1.155 is amended to provide expedited examination of US‑designated international design applications where the international design application has been published pursuant to Hague Agreement Article 10(3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides a mechanism for faster prosecution when the international application has been published under the Hague rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty of disclosure for US‑designated international design applications (§ 1.56)
rubrics_metrics.description: International design applications which designate the US are subject to the duty of disclosure under § 1.56.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants and counsel must comply with the same duty to disclose known material information to the USPTO as applies to domestic filings when the US is designated.

rubrics_metrics.name: No fee discounts from Hague Agreement
rubrics_metrics.description: The Hague Agreement does not offer discounts for its use and therefore does not save applicants money in fees associated with each jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although filing is centralized, applicants must still pay the fees associated with each jurisdiction they wish to enter; cost savings from bypassing local counsel may be possible in some jurisdictions but Hague itself does not reduce official fees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hague does not change national application/drawing/examination standards
rubrics_metrics.description: The Hague Agreement does not affect the application requirements, drawing standards, or examination standards of any of the member jurisdictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants must meet each designated jurisdiction's substantive requirements; an international filing via Hague does not relax or harmonize local substantive standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: US-specific strict examination standards and risks
rubrics_metrics.description: The US has particularly strict design examination standards, especially regarding specification and claim language and the content and quality of drawings; there is sensitivity to adding new matter and difficulty correcting rejected applications once on file.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of these stricter US rules, entering the US with an international application can be risky if the application was not drafted with US requirements in mind; corrections after filing may be difficult or impossible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendation to consult US counsel before entering US
rubrics_metrics.description: It may be prudent to confer with US counsel before filing international design applications that are intended to enter the US to guard against uncorrectable international application defects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pre-filing coordination with US counsel can help ensure the international application meets US standards and avoids defects that cannot be fixed later during US examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparing applications to meet US requirements as a global strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: An international design application prepared with a goal of meeting US requirements will most likely be acceptable in most of the other Hague Agreement member jurisdictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drafting to the highest (US) standard can serve as a conservative strategy to maximize acceptance across multiple jurisdictions, at the possible cost of greater upfront drafting effort and expense.
